lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A safe area, the United Nations called it. A resolution passed, votes counted, the words written down: free from any armed attack.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On July eleventh, nineteen ninety five, the general commanding the army outside that safe area walked into its town on camera and said the time had come to take revenge.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Six hundred peacekeepers were stationed inside it. They did not fire a shot.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A resolution is a sentence. It cannot stop a bulldozer.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Srebrenica genocide. July eleventh to twenty second, nineteen ninety five.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: By July of nineteen ninety five, the siege of Sarajevo has been running for one thousand four hundred twenty five days, the longest in modern European history. Shelling and sniper fire from the hills above the city have killed eleven thousand five hundred forty one people. One thousand six hundred and one of them are children.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The war began in April of nineteen ninety two, when Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence and Bosnian Serb forces, armed by the Yugoslav army under Slobodan Milosevic, moved to carve an ethnically pure Serb republic out of the country.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Srebrenica, a mining town in the east, has held out as a Bosniak enclave inside Serb held territory since almost the start of it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Dutch battalion holding the enclave has been low on fuel, food, and ammunition for weeks, boxed in by an army that controls the only road in, and it has lost dozens of its men, taken hostage.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: When Mladic's forces advance, the Dutch commander, Thom Karremans, asks for NATO air support. Two aircraft appear on July eleventh, drop a handful of bombs, and are withdrawn after the Serbs threaten to kill the hostages and the refugees crowding the base.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: That afternoon, Mladic walks into the empty town. A camera is rolling.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Ratko Mladic, commander of the Bosnian Serb Army, turns to the camera and says this.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The time has come to take revenge on the Turks in this region.

segments.author: Ratko Mladic
segments.work: Filmed statement on entering Srebrenica, later a trial exhibit at the ICTY

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The people he means are sheltering by the thousands at the Dutch compound in Potocari, the battery factory where the peacekeepers are based. Within a day, Bosnian Serb soldiers begin pulling men and boys out of that crowd.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Over five days, Bosnian Serb forces separate men and boys from their families at the battery factory. Boys are judged by height, not by age.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Between twenty five thousand and thirty thousand women, children, and elderly people are put on buses and driven out within seventy two hours.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The men, roughly eight thousand of them, go to fields, schools, and warehouses. At a warehouse in Kravica, on July thirteenth, more than a thousand men are packed inside and killed with grenades and gunfire through the windows.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: At Orahovac, at Petkovci, at a farm called Branjevo, at a cultural center in Pilica, prisoners are bused out, lined up, and shot. The dead are pushed into pits by excavator.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Drazen Erdemovic was one of eight men doing the shooting at Branjevo that day. This is what he told the tribunal about the ones who tried to refuse.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: They told me that if I felt sorry for them, I should line up with them so they could kill me too.

segments.author: Drazen Erdemovic
segments.work: Testimony before the ICTY on the executions at Branjevo Military Farm

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Erdemovic later estimated that he alone killed seventy men that day. He was one shooter, at one farm, of eight running at once.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Ten thousand to fifteen thousand men do not wait in the fields. They go into the forest instead, trying to reach Bosnian government lines at a town called Nezuk, more than sixty kilometers away.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: For days the column is shelled, split apart, and ambushed. Some surrender to soldiers in stolen UN uniforms and are executed; others die of thirst and gunfire.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Survivors give it a name: the death march.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Fewer than half of them reach the other side.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The killing is not the end of what the perpetrators do. Bosnian Serb units return to the graves with excavators and move the bodies, breaking single corpses apart across scattered secondary sites, so that no one grave will ever hold the whole crime.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The International Commission on Missing Persons has since reassembled more than six thousand nine hundred victims from bone fragments, matched by DNA, from more than ninety grave sites. The graves are still being found.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Twelve years later, the International Court of Justice rules on what those graves held.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: These were acts of genocide, committed by members of the VRS in and around Srebrenica from about 13 July 1995.

segments.author: International Court of Justice
segments.work: Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro, Judgment

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Genocide Convention was written in nineteen forty eight, after the Holocaust, under the words never again. Forty seven years later, eight thousand men and boys died inside a United Nations safe area, in Europe.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Five accounts of what happened at Srebrenica and in the war around it. One of them is not a rival version of events. It is the record of what the killers said about their own crime while they were still denying it, set down here to be answered, not balanced.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Hasan Nuhanovic worked as an interpreter for the Dutch battalion. On July thirteenth, Dutch soldiers ordered his mother, father, and younger brother off the UN compound at Potocari, into the hands of the waiting Bosnian Serb forces. He kept his UN badge and was allowed to stay. He never saw his family alive again. In two thousand thirteen the Supreme Court of the Netherlands ruled that the Dutch state was liable for their deaths.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In two thousand one the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia convicted General Radislav Krstic of genocide, the first genocide conviction on European soil. It later convicted Mladic, and upheld a life sentence for Karadzic. Twenty men were tried for Srebrenica in total.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Judge Fouad Riad, hearing the tribunal's first evidence on Srebrenica in nineteen ninety five, puts it this way.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: These are truly scenes from hell, written on the darkest pages of human history.

segments.title: Bosniak Survivors and the Legal Record

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Resolution eight nineteen declared Srebrenica a safe area in April of nineteen ninety three, but sent no army capable of defending it. The task fell to Dutchbat, roughly six hundred lightly armed peacekeepers, holding a mandate written for peacekeeping, not war.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Some twenty thousand to twenty five thousand civilians fled to the Dutch compound at Potocari, with shelter and food for only a fraction of them.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In nineteen ninety nine, the Secretary-General's own report on the fall of Srebrenica said this.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Through error, misjudgement and an inability to recognize the scope of the evil confronting us, we failed to do our part to help save the people of Srebrenica from the Serb campaign of mass murder.

segments.title: The UN Safe Area and the Dutch Peacekeepers

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Denial did not begin after the genocide. It was built into it. Bosnian Serb units broke the bodies apart across scattered secondary graves for exactly this reason, so that no single grave would ever prove the whole crime.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The claims that followed ran to a script. The numbers are inflated. The men died in combat. The killing was revenge for raids that Bosniak fighters under Naser Oric had launched on Serb villages years earlier.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In two thousand five, a video surfaced showing a paramilitary unit called the Scorpions marching six bound prisoners from Srebrenica into a field and shooting them. It was broadcast across Serbia.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In two thousand four, the government of Republika Srpska issued its own report naming the perpetrators. In two thousand eighteen, under Milorad Dodik, its assembly revoked that report. Serbia's parliament apologized for the crime in two thousand ten, and would not use the word genocide.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Dodik has since put it this way.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The Srebrenica genocide is a fabricated myth.

segments.title: Genocide Denial versus the International Juridical Finding

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Every July eleventh, green coffins go up the hillside at Potocari and into the ground, one row further than the year before. Some hold a nearly complete body; others, only a few bones, all that DNA could match.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Munira Subasic and Hatidza Mehmedovic led the women who organized as the Mothers of Srebrenica, turning grief into a legal and political force. Mehmedovic lost her husband and both sons, and lived in Srebrenica until her own death in two thousand eighteen, among neighbors who still denied her sons were dead.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: They took the Netherlands and the United Nations to court, in The Hague and at the European Court of Human Rights. The Dutch state was found partly responsible. The United Nations claimed immunity, and kept it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Each year, the Mars Mira, the Peace March, retraces the death route in reverse, tens of thousands walking three days from Nezuk to Potocari to arrive for the burials.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: After the Mladic verdict in twenty seventeen, Munira Subasic said this.

lines.speaker: F
lines.text: We mothers will never forgive, and we will never forget.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The phrase entered global use in nineteen ninety two: ethnic cleansing. It was not a euphemism invented in the West. It was the perpetrators' own term for the objective, removing a population from a territory by terror.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The method ran across Bosnia from the war's first weeks, well before Srebrenica. In the Prijedor region, non Serbs were driven into camps at Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, exposed to the world in August of nineteen ninety two when journalists filmed emaciated men behind barbed wire.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In Visegrad, families were locked in houses on the Drina and burned alive. In Foca, rape was organized as an instrument of war; the tribunal's Kunarac judgment in two thousand one first defined rape as a crime against humanity in international law.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In two thousand seven, the International Court of Justice applied the strict legal definition and found that only the killings at Srebrenica crossed the threshold of genocide, while it ruled the broader campaign was ethnic cleansing that did not.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A United Nations commission chaired by Cherif Bassiouni catalogued the pattern in nineteen ninety four and gave ethnic cleansing its working definition.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Ethnic cleansing is a purposeful policy designed by one ethnic or religious group to remove by violent and terror-inspiring means the civilian population of another ethnic or religious group from certain geographic areas.

segments.title: Scholarship on Ethnic Cleansing in the Yugoslav Wars

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: What each of these does not carry.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The survivors' account has the least power to shape any peace that follows, and the least incentive to be measured about a government that also did not always fight this war by its own rules.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The peacekeepers' account is a story about a warning system that failed above the battalion's head, and it says less about a compound built to shelter only a fraction of twenty five thousand people.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The denial account calls the numbers inflated and the dead combat losses, and it says nothing about why the graves needed digging up a second time, if there was nothing in the first ones worth hiding.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The mothers' account refuses to let the number eight thousand become an abstraction, and it is also the account least able to weigh, from inside its own grief, what a six hundred man battalion could have done differently at that gate.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And the scholarship draws the line of genocide exactly at Srebrenica, a legal boundary the International Court of Justice itself drew, while the camps at Omarska and the burnings at Visegrad sit one step outside the word the law reserves for the worst thing it names.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Munira Subasic searched for her son Nermin for years. His remains were found in pieces, across two graves.
